summary: Describes how the zone identifier of an IPv6 scoped address can be written in a literal IPv6 address and in a URI that contains one. It updates the URI syntax of RFC 3986. It was replaced by RFC 9844.

plainLanguage.summary: Some addresses only make sense on one local network, like room 5 means nothing without the building. This says how to write the building part in a web link.

questions: how to put an ipv6 zone id in a url
what is the percent sign in ipv6 addresses

subtitle: Syntax for writing IPv6 link-local addresses with their interface in a web link

tldr.problem: IPv6 scoped addresses include a zone identifier that specifies which local network interface they belong to, but there is no standard way to write them in URIs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how to append a zone identifier to an IPv6 literal in a URI by using %25 (percent-encoded percent sign) followed by the zone ID, such as http://[fe80::a%25en1].
tldr.outcome: Users can now include zone identifiers in URIs for debugging with link-local addresses, and the syntax respects the established URI encoding rules.

today: RFC 6874 is a Proposed Standard that defined a syntax for zone identifiers in URIs. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9844, which updates the IPv6 zone identifier specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses that are limited to a single link, called link-local addresses, include a zone identifier that specifies which network interface on a host they apply to. For example, fe80::a%en1 means the address fe80::a on the en1 interface. This notation is defined in RFC 4007.

When these scoped addresses need to appear in a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), such as a web browser URL, the RFC 3986 URI syntax did not define how to represent the zone identifier. Some browsers handled this inconsistently or used nonstandard syntax. RFC 6874 updates the URI specification to provide a formal syntax that allows zone identifiers while respecting URI encoding rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses only work on one cable in your computer. This shows how to write which cable you mean when you put the address in a web link.

sections.title: The Syntax for Zone Identifiers in URIs
sections.content:
According to RFC 6874, a zone identifier is appended to a literal IPv6 address inside square brackets by percent-encoding the percent sign itself. The character % is always an escape character in URIs, so the zone identifier en1 becomes %25en1. A complete example is http://[fe80::a%25en1]/.

The zone ID SHOULD contain only unreserved URI characters, but if the operating system uses other characters in zone or interface identifiers, they MAY be percent-encoded. The formal syntax is: IPv6addrz = IPv6address "%25" ZoneID, where ZoneID is one or more unreserved or percent-encoded characters.
sections.plainLanguage: To write a zone ID in a web link, you write % as %25, then the zone ID. So eth0 becomes %25eth0 in the link.

sections.title: Scope and Usage
sections.content:
Zone identifiers in URIs are intended mainly for debugging and diagnostic purposes, such as when a user needs to reach a specific interface for fault diagnosis. They are meaningful only on the host where they originate; zone identifiers have no meaning on any other node and are purely local to the system that defines them.

The syntax is particularly useful for reaching link-local addresses under the prefix fe80::/10, which are the most common scope-limited addresses. The RFC recommends that implementations limit the use of this format to well-defined usages such as sending to link-local addresses and that browsers remove zone IDs from outgoing HTTP requests, since zone identifiers have only local significance at the sending host.
sections.plainLanguage: You only use this format when you are trying to reach something on your own computer's cables. If you send a link with a zone ID to someone else, their computer won't understand it.

sections.title: Security and Browser Behavior
sections.content:
The main security risk is that a zone identifier in a URI could communicate a misleading interface designation, as noted in RFC 4007. To limit this risk, implementations MUST NOT allow use of this format except for well-defined usages such as sending to link-local addresses. HTTP clients, proxies, and other intermediaries MUST remove any zone identifier from an outgoing URI, since it has no meaning outside the originating host.

Web browsers should accept the syntax but should not include zone IDs in HTTP requests. For user convenience, browsers MAY accept bare percent signs when they are clearly not valid percent-encoding, allowing users to copy diagnostic output like ping fe80::a%en1 directly into a URL, though this must be converted to the formal syntax %25en1 before use in a protocol message.
sections.plainLanguage: This format is just for your computer talking to itself. Don't send a zone ID to someone else's computer, and don't put it in a web page that goes to a server. Browsers should help you type it in, but they should clean it up before sending anything.
